The Charlotte Hornets and Brandon Miller have agreed to a five-year, $209 million extension to his rookie contract, ESPN's Shams Charania reports — a deal cementing the No. 2 overall pick in the 2023 NBA Draft as one of the cornerstones of the ongoing effort to build a consistent contender in the Queen City.
 The two sides agreed to the deal Monday, hours ahead of a deadline for players from Miller's draft class to sign an extension. Had they not reached agreement on a deal, Miller would have played the upcoming season on a team option, then gone into next offseason as a restricted free agent.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Instead, Miller is under contract for five more seasons at $41.8 million per year after playing the first four seasons of his rookie contract for a total of $49.4 million.
 The former Alabama standout bounced back from an injury-wracked sophomore season to turn in a stellar third campaign, averaging 20.2 points, 4.9 rebounds, 3.3 assists and 1 steal in 30.3 minutes per game with a career-best .574 true shooting percentage (which factors in 2-point, 3-point and free-throw accuracy). Miller was one of only a dozen wing players to hit those marks last season, according to Stathead ; 10 of the other 11 members of the list are All-Star and All-NBA honorees. (We see you, Trey Murphy III.)
 The list of wings to produce like that by their age-23 season includes some of the brightest young perimeter players in the league in recent years — names like Giannis Antetokounmpo, Kevin Durant, James Harden, Jayson Tatum, Anthony Edwards, Devin Booker and Jalen Williams. That's the kind of company the Hornets are betting — and betting big — that Miller can continue to keep, developing into the kind of perennial All-Star and All-NBA candidate who can lift Charlotte into the ranks of the league's elite teams.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement After missing most of the first month of the season following a left shoulder subluxation , Miller played a significant role in helping the Hornets climb out of an early hole to become one of the hottest teams in the NBA over the final few months. LaMelo Ball's high-octane playmaking and rookie Kon Knueppel's deadeye marksmanship drew the most headlines, but the 6-foot-7 Miller's all-around play on the wing — as a spot-up threat on the weak side of the primary action, as a complementary pick-and-roll ball-handler, as a speed demon sprinting the floor in transition, and as an improved multipositional perimeter defender — helped tie it all together for head coach Charles Lee's squad, which boasted the NBA's sixth-best record and second -best net rating after Christmas, according to Cleaning the Glass .
 "Definitely [want to do] everything I can do to win a basketball game, whether that's guarding the best player, guarding a player that can't shoot or [has a] lower percentage, I take pride in that two-way mindset," Miller told Rod Boone of the Charlotte Observer last season . "It's been going great this year. We get a lot of wins when everybody's locked into that two-way mindset. So, just keep having that mindset."
 That second-half surge led the Hornets to the verge of the postseason, with a play-in victory over the Miami Heat followed by a loss to the Orlando Magic in their second play-in contest. But despite coming within arm's reach of the franchise's first playoff appearance since 2016 , and despite playing the most exciting and energizing brand of ball that Hornets fans have seen in ages, Charlotte's brass elected to reorient the roster this summer, dealing Ball and guard Josh Green to the Minnesota Timberwolves in exchange for sweet-shooting forward Naz Reid, an unprotected 2033 first-round pick, swap rights on Minnesota's firsts in 2028, 2029 and 2030, and second-round picks in 2029, 2032 and 2033.
 Whatever rationale you ascribe to the trade — the Hornets' front office not believing the roster was quite as good as that torrid second half suggested, seizing the opportunity to get out of the Ball business after he'd had a healthy season for the first time in four years, believing Coby White could replace most of Ball's production at a substantially lower dollar figure — it also represented, to some degree, a bet on Miller (and Knueppel) being able to expand his offensive game and shot-creation capabilities, and grow into the centerpiece of a winning organization, if given the opportunity.
 "Brandon, I think everyone would agree he's an enormous talent," Hornets executive vice president of basketball operations Jeff Peterson told reporters this summer . "He showed a tremendous amount of growth last season battling through an injury, but was able to continue to persevere and again help us achieve some results that made our fan base and us very, very excited, proud. [...] Of course, everyone knows he's skilled and athletic, and he has a true desire to win and continue to get better. So could not be more excited to be going into next season with Brandon Miller on our squad."
 To make the sort of impact that Peterson and the rest of Charlotte's braintrust believe he can, Miller will need to stay on the floor. He had surgery on that troublesome left shoulder after the season and spent the summer rehabilitating it, aiming to enter the 2026-27 campaign stronger, more stable and better able to take on the additional on- and off-court responsibilities awaiting him in Ball's absence, as one of the leaders on a team with its sights set on ending the NBA's longest ongoing postseason drought .
 "Do I know if we are going to be good or great?" Miller said back in August . "I know we are going to be a hard-working team. It's not about who makes the most shots. It's about who can play consistently at 110% every night. I think that's one thing we are going to take pride in."
